script.opening: "I’m at my wits’ end, doctor. Noah screams inconsolably for hours, mostly in the evenings, going red and pulling his legs up, and nothing settles him. He’s six weeks old. He feeds and is gaining weight, but I’m exhausted and terrified there’s something seriously wrong with him."

facts.text: Started at about 2 weeks old. Most days, 3–4 hours each evening, from about 6pm. Goes red, clenches his fists, pulls his legs up. Settles eventually and sleeps. Content between episodes.
Bottle-fed formula since 2 weeks (breastfeeding was difficult). Feeds well. Health visitor weighed him 3 days ago: "on his line, gaining nicely". Small possets after feeds, not forceful, never green.

No fever. Not floppy or drowsy. No blood in nappies; normal yellow stools. Plenty of wet nappies. No rash, no breathing problems, no fits. Soft spot not bulging. No swelling in the groin. Cry is loud, not high-pitched or weak. Mum can undress him on camera if asked — he looks pink and well.
Born at 39 weeks, normal delivery, 3.4 kg. Newborn checks normal. No medicines. Mum has tried gripe water.

Exhausted; partner, Dan, works nights. "I feel like I’m failing him." Worried all the time, down sometimes when he won’t stop. No thoughts of harming herself or Noah: "No, never. I just cry with him." Not much help — her mum lives 2 hours away. Had anxiety as a teenager.

Tired, tearful, anxious. Keep looking for a medical cause. Ask "Should I change his milk or get some drops?" Feel relieved if the doctor asks about you and listens. Be surprised that it’s OK to put him down safely and walk away for a few minutes.

ice.ideas: "Something must be hurting him — maybe his tummy, or an allergy to the milk."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her own exhaustion and fear that she is failing; feels isolated with Dan on nights.
ice.expectations: "Something to stop the crying — a different milk or drops."

cues: "I’m exhausted" — explore her wellbeing, mood and support.
"I feel like I’m failing him" — needs validation and a check on coping.
"Should I change his milk?" — expectation to discuss.

checkpoints.text: Recognises INFANTILE COLIC — excessive paroxysmal (often evening) crying in an otherwise well, thriving infant (knowing the rule of 3s is a research definition, not a threshold), resolving by ~3–4 months — as a diagnosis of exclusion

EXCLUDES red flags/other causes by history and a full undressed EXAMINATION face to face — poor feeding/faltering weight, fever (38 °C or more under 3 months → same-day paediatric assessment, NICE NG143), bile vomiting, blood in stool, lethargy, tense fontanelle, hernia/torsion, hair-tourniquet, CMPA, GORD
REASSURES that colic is benign and self-limiting and not the parent’s fault, once red flags are excluded

Gives practical SOOTHING/feeding advice and avoids routine medications/formula changes unless a specific cause is suspected (limited evidence for simethicone/probiotics etc.; no acid suppression for crying alone, NICE NG1; CMPA only with other features, NICE CG116)

SUPPORTS the exhausted PARENT — validates the toll, asks about parental coping, low mood and anxiety (NICE CG192), mobilises support, and gives the ICON safety advice (it’s okay to put the baby down safely and take a break; NEVER shake the baby)
Acknowledges the enormous strain and the fear that something is wrong, validates her distress, and reassures without dismissing
Explains the diagnosis and plan clearly, checks understanding, and engages support around her

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent review (fever, poor feeding/weight, bile vomiting, blood in stool, lethargy), parental-wellbeing follow-up/health visitor, never-shake advice, and review — red-flag exclusion + reassurance + parental support

worked.txt: "You’re absolutely right to bring him — I need to examine Noah fully undressed, so I’d like to see you both face to face today to make sure there’s nothing being missed. … (At the face-to-face check:) He’s feeding, gaining weight, his tummy’s soft, no hernia, fontanelle’s fine, and I’ve checked his fingers, toes and nappy area. He’s a well, thriving baby."

"What you’re describing — inconsolable evening crying, legs drawn up, in a healthy baby this age — is colic. It’s extremely common, it’s not dangerous, and crucially it’s nothing you’re doing wrong. It typically settles by three to four months."

"Some things can help in the moment — holding and gentle rocking, white noise, movement, winding, a calm dim room. I’d be cautious about over-the-counter remedies or changing formula, as the evidence is limited unless there’s a specific cause like a milk allergy, which I don’t think fits here."
"Now — how are YOU doing? This is genuinely exhausting and can wear anyone down. Are you getting any rest or help? How’s your mood?" (Listens, screens for PND.)

"One really important thing: if he’s crying and you feel overwhelmed, it’s completely okay to put him down somewhere safe like his cot, step away for a few minutes to breathe, and come back. And never, ever shake him — even gentle shaking can harm a baby."

"Come back urgently if he develops a fever, feeds poorly, vomits green, has blood in his nappy, or becomes floppy or unusually sleepy. And let’s get the health visitor involved to support you — I’d like to check on you both again."

f.learning: INFANTILE COLIC is excessive, paroxysmal, often EVENING crying in an otherwise WELL, THRIVING infant — often described by Wessel’s "rule of 3s" (>3 hours/day, >3 days/week, for >3 weeks), a research definition rather than a diagnostic threshold (the Rome IV criteria, international, require no set number of hours) — with drawing up of the legs, typically beginning in the early weeks and resolving by ~3–4 months; it is a clinical diagnosis of EXCLUSION in an otherwise healthy baby. The key task is to EXCLUDE red flags/other causes by history and a full undressed examination face to face (temperature, weight on the chart, skin for bruising): poor feeding or faltering weight, fever/sepsis (NICE NG143: 38 °C or more under 3 months is a red feature needing same-day paediatric assessment; NICE NG254 if sepsis is possible), vomiting (especially bile-stained — obstruction), blood in stool, lethargy/floppiness, a bulging/tense fontanelle, an incarcerated hernia or testicular torsion, a hair-tourniquet (finger/toe/penis), corneal foreign body, cow’s-milk protein allergy (only with other features, NICE CG116) and GORD (no acid suppression for crying or regurgitation alone in an otherwise healthy infant, NICE NG1) — a thriving, well, examined baby with no red flags supports colic. Once red flags are excluded, REASSURE that colic is benign and self-limiting, usually settling by 3–4 months and not the parent’s fault, which directly addresses the fear that "something is seriously wrong". Give practical soothing/feeding advice (holding/rocking, white noise, movement, winding, a calm environment), while noting that evidence for specific treatments (simethicone, lactase drops, probiotics, formula/dietary changes) is limited — avoid routine medications or formula changes unless a specific cause (e.g. CMPA) is suspected and then trial appropriately. Crucially, SUPPORT the exhausted, anxious PARENT: acknowledge the enormous toll, validate distress, ask about parental coping, low mood and anxiety (NICE CG192), mobilise support (partner/family/health visitor), and give the ICON ("Babies cry, you can cope") safety advice that it is okay to place the baby safely down and take a break if overwhelmed and to NEVER shake the baby; any unexplained bruise in a non-mobile baby needs safeguarding action (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023). The skill is red-flag exclusion + reassurance + parental support, with safety-netting and follow-up.

knowledge.summary: Long bouts of evening crying with legs drawn up in a 6-week-old who is feeding, gaining weight and otherwise well is infantile colic, a diagnosis made only after a full examination excludes other causes. The real work is reassurance and supporting an exhausted parent, including the never-shake message.

points.t: Prolonged, hard-to-soothe crying in a well, thriving baby, usually starting in the first weeks, often worse in the evenings, and settling by about 3–4 months. Wessel’s ‘rule of three’ (over 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for 3 weeks) is a research definition; the Rome IV criteria (international) do not require a set number of hours. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Ask about feeding, weight, vomiting (bilious = obstruction), stools and blood, fever, breathing, rash and drowsiness. Examine fully undressed: temperature, weight on the chart, fontanelle, abdomen, hernial orifices and testes, fingers, toes and penis for a hair tourniquet, eyes, skin for bruising. NICE NG143 [1]: a temperature of 38 °C or more under 3 months is a red feature needing same-day paediatric assessment; use NICE NG254 [2] if sepsis is possible.

Crying alone is not a reason to treat reflux: NICE NG1 [3] advises against acid-suppressing drugs for regurgitation as an isolated symptom in an otherwise healthy infant, and reserves a trial for regurgitation with other features. Consider cow’s milk allergy only with other features such as eczema, vomiting, diarrhoea, blood in stool or faltering growth, assessed per NICE CG116 [4].

Explain that colic is common, not harmful and not caused by anything the parent has done. Holding, gentle movement, white noise, a calm room and winding may help. Evidence for over-the-counter remedies and formula changes is limited; avoid routine formula changes without a specific reason.
Persistent crying is exhausting and is linked with parental low mood. NICE CG192 [5]: consider asking about depression and anxiety. Involve the health visitor and family support.

Crying is a recognised trigger for abusive head trauma. Give the ICON [6] message: crying is normal, comforting helps, it is okay to put the baby down safely and walk away for a few minutes, and never shake a baby. Any unexplained bruise in a non-mobile baby needs safeguarding action [7].

dg.d: Open start; greeted parent and baby; let her describe the crying and her fear.
Her exhaustion, support at home and sense of failing explored.
Full undressed examination: temperature, weight plotted, fontanelle, abdomen, hernias, testes, hair tourniquet, skin.
Colic versus infection, obstruction, hernia or torsion, hair tourniquet, reflux, cow’s milk allergy and injury.
Asked about fever, bilious vomiting, blood in stool, lethargy and cry; NICE NG143 fever threshold under 3 months.
Named infantile colic only after examination.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Reassurance; practical soothing; no routine drops or formula change (NICE NG1, NICE CG116 if allergy features).
Parental mood and anxiety asked (NICE CG192); health visitor; ICON never-shake advice.
Red-flag safety-net; teach-back of the coping plan; review in 2 weeks.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “exhausted and terrified” and turned the consultation to her wellbeing.
Idea (something wrong), concern (a serious illness and her coping), expectation (reassurance and help).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — her own exhaustion and fear that she is failing; feels isolated with Dan on nights — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Khan. You must be Noah’s mum — Hannah, is it? And this must be Noah. What’s been happening?
model.why: Open start, greets parent and baby

model.text: I’m at my wits’ end, doctor. Noah screams inconsolably for hours, mostly in the evenings, going red and pulling his legs up, and nothing settles him. He’s six weeks old. He feeds and is gaining weight, but I’m exhausted and terrified there’s something seriously wrong with him.
You’ve done the right thing bringing him. I’ll ask some questions, examine him properly, and then we’ll talk about him and about you.
How long has this been going on, and how much of the day is he crying?
A few weeks. Several hours most days, worst in the evening.
Between those spells, is he his usual self, alert and feeding well?
Yes, he feeds well and he’s gaining weight.
Has he had a temperature, been sick, especially anything green, or had any blood in his nappy?
model.why: Red flags: fever, bilious vomiting, blood in stool

model.text: No, nothing like that. Normal nappies.
Has he been floppy or unusually sleepy, had any breathing problems, or a rash or dry skin patches?
No. His skin’s fine.
Does the cry ever sound different, high-pitched or weak?
No, just loud.
Now, how are you doing? This sounds really hard.
(tearful) I’m shattered. I feel like I’m failing him.

You’re not failing him. You’re looking after him and you brought him in. Over the last month, have you often felt down or hopeless, or lost interest in things? And have you felt nervous or unable to stop worrying?
model.why: Depression and anxiety identification questions (NICE CG192)

model.text: Worried, yes, all the time. Down sometimes, when he won’t stop.
Thank you for telling me. When he’s screaming and you’re exhausted, have you ever felt so overwhelmed that you worried you might hurt him?
model.why: Asks directly and safely about risk

model.text: No, never. I just cry with him.
Who’s around to help you at the moment?
Not as much as I’d like.

Let me examine Noah fully undressed. (Weighs and plots him, checks temperature, fontanelle, heart and chest, abdomen, groins and testes, hips, eyes, skin, and fingers, toes and penis for a hair tourniquet.) Temperature is normal, he’s following his weight line, his tummy is soft, no hernia, his skin is clear and there’s nothing wrapped round his fingers or toes.
model.why: Full examination to exclude other causes

model.text: Noah is a healthy, thriving baby. What you’re describing is colic. It’s very common, it isn’t harmful, and it isn’t caused by anything you’re doing. It usually eases by around three to four months.
Should I change his milk or get some drops?

There isn’t good evidence that drops or changing milk help colic, and nothing today suggests a milk allergy. Holding him close, gentle rocking, a car or pram ride, white noise and a dim, quiet room can all help.
model.why: Practical soothing; avoids routine remedies or formula change

model.text: The most important thing I’ll say today: if you feel yourself getting overwhelmed, it is completely okay to put him down safely on his back in his cot, close the door, and take a few minutes to calm down. Crying won’t hurt him. And never shake a baby, even gently, because it can cause serious brain injury.
I didn’t know it was okay to walk away.

It is. I’d also like the health visitor to visit you this week, and I’ll give you the ICON information. Because you’ve been feeling low and worried, I’d like to see you again to talk about how you are.
model.why: Health visitor, written information, mood follow-up

model.text: Bring him back urgently or call 111 if he has a temperature of 38 or more, stops feeding, is sick green, has blood in his nappy, becomes floppy or very sleepy, or his cry changes. What will you do tonight if the crying gets too much?
model.why: Specific safety-net and teach-back of the coping plan

model.text: Put him in his cot safely, step out for a few minutes, then go back. And ring if he gets a temperature or goes floppy.
Exactly. I’ll see you in two weeks, sooner if you need.

social.t: Evening crying and night feeds leave parents exhausted; practical help and rest breaks matter.
Ask who can help. Family, friends and local parent groups can take turns.

legal.t: Crying is a trigger for abusive head trauma. Any bruise or unexplained injury in a non-mobile baby needs referral under local safeguarding procedures (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).
Confirm that the adult attending has parental responsibility or consent to bring the baby.

professional.t: The consultation is about the baby and the parent. Record the parent’s mood and any support arranged (NICE CG192).
Avoid prescribing for normal crying; crying without regurgitation and other features is not an indication for acid suppression (NICE NG1).

community.t: Can visit, weigh, support feeding and screen mood.
ICON: Babies cry, you can cope (iconcope.org) gives parents simple coping messages.

redFlags: Temperature 38 °C or more under 3 months (NICE NG143)
Bilious vomiting, blood in stool or a distended abdomen
Poor feeding, faltering weight, floppiness or drowsiness
High-pitched or weak cry, bulging fontanelle
Groin or scrotal swelling; hair tourniquet
psychosocial: Parental exhaustion and sense of failure
ice: Concern: a missed illness and her own coping

playbook.diagnosis: “Noah has colic. I’ve examined him fully and he’s a healthy, thriving baby.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Colic means long bouts of crying in a well baby. We don’t fully know why it happens, but it isn’t harmful, it isn’t anything you’ve done, and it usually settles by three to four months.”

management.reflectIce: “You were terrified something serious was wrong. I’ve checked him from head to toe, and he’s well. Now I want to make sure you’re okay too.”
management.psychosocial: Validate her exhaustion; ask about mood and anxiety; explicit permission to put him down safely.
sharedPlan: Reassurance and soothing strategies; no routine drops or formula changes
ICON information; never-shake and walk-away advice
Health visitor visit; review of parental mood (NICE CG192)
safetyNet: Temperature 38 °C or more, poor feeding, green vomit, blood in nappy, floppiness or change in cry: urgent review or 111
Feeling unable to cope or low mood: contact the practice or health visitor the same day

pitfalls.intro: The diagnosis is easy; the marks are in how safely you reach it and how well you look after the parent. Candidates fail by skipping the examination, by medicalising crying, and by never asking about the mother.

items.why: Colic is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection, hernia, torsion and hair tourniquet must be ruled out.
items.fix: Examine fully undressed and plot the weight.

items.fail: Prescribing drops, reflux medicine or a new formula.
items.why: Evidence is limited, and crying alone is not an indication for acid suppression (NICE NG1).
items.fix: Reassure and give soothing strategies; consider allergy only with other features (NICE CG116).

items.why: Crying is a recognised trigger for abusive head trauma.
items.fix: Give the ICON message, including permission to walk away safely.

items.why: Her exhaustion and anxiety are the hidden agenda, and postnatal mood matters (NICE CG192).
items.fix: Ask how she is, screen mood and anxiety, and arrange support.

items.why: Early reassurance sounds dismissive and may be wrong.
items.fix: Examine first, then reassure with the findings.

items.why: A febrile baby under 3 months needs same-day assessment (NICE NG143).
items.fix: Name the red flags and the 38 °C threshold, and book review.

Pattern, feeding, weight, fever, vomiting, stools, lethargy, rash, cry.
Mood and anxiety questions; ask about overwhelm and support.
Full undressed examination including hair tourniquet. Name colic and reassure.
Soothing; no routine remedies; ICON and never shake; health visitor; red-flag safety-net; teach-back; review.

wordPics.fail: Calls it colic without examining; prescribes drops or changes formula; never asks how the mother is; no never-shake advice.
wordPics.pass: Screens red flags, examines fully, names colic and reassures, gives soothing advice and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks about her mood and anxiety and about feeling overwhelmed; gives the never-shake and walk-away message clearly; involves the health visitor; teaches back a coping plan; books her own follow-up.

avoid.dont: “All babies cry, he’ll grow out of it.”
avoid.instead: “I’ve examined him fully and he’s healthy. This is colic, it’s common and it isn’t your fault.”
avoid.why: Reassurance lands only after proper examination, and dismissal leaves her alone with the strain.

avoid.instead: “Changing milk doesn’t usually help colic, and nothing suggests an allergy.”
avoid.why: Formula changes without allergy features add cost and worry without evidence (NICE CG116).

avoid.instead: “If it gets too much, put him down safely in his cot and take a few minutes. Never shake him.”
avoid.why: Explicit permission to walk away and the never-shake message protect the baby (ICON).

Persistent crying is exhausting and is linked with parental low mood. NICE CG192 [5]: consider asking about depression and anxiety. Involve the health visitor and family support.

Crying is a recognised trigger for abusive head trauma. Give the ICON [6] message: crying is normal, comforting helps, it is okay to put the baby down safely and walk away for a few minutes, and never shake a baby. Any unexplained bruise in a non-mobile baby needs safeguarding action [7].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; greeted parent and baby; let her describe the crying and her fear.
Her exhaustion, support at home and sense of failing explored.
Picked up “exhausted and terrified” and turned the consultation to her wellbeing.
Idea (something wrong), concern (a serious illness and her coping), expectation (reassurance and help).
Full undressed examination: temperature, weight plotted, fontanelle, abdomen, hernias, testes, hair tourniquet, skin.
Colic versus infection, obstruction, hernia or torsion, hair tourniquet, reflux, cow’s milk allergy and injury.
Asked about fever, bilious vomiting, blood in stool, lethargy and cry; NICE NG143 fever threshold under 3 months.
Named infantile colic only after examination.
Reassurance; practical soothing; no routine drops or formula change (NICE NG1, NICE CG116 if allergy features).
Parental mood and anxiety asked (NICE CG192); health visitor; ICON never-shake advice.
Red-flag safety-net; teach-back of the coping plan; review in 2 weeks.

social.t: Evening crying and night feeds leave parents exhausted; practical help and rest breaks matter.
Ask who can help. Family, friends and local parent groups can take turns.

legal.t: Crying is a trigger for abusive head trauma. Any bruise or unexplained injury in a non-mobile baby needs referral under local safeguarding procedures (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).
Confirm that the adult attending has parental responsibility or consent to bring the baby.

professional.t: The consultation is about the baby and the parent. Record the parent’s mood and any support arranged (NICE CG192).
Avoid prescribing for normal crying; crying without regurgitation and other features is not an indication for acid suppression (NICE NG1).

community.t: Can visit, weigh, support feeding and screen mood.
ICON: Babies cry, you can cope (iconcope.org) gives parents simple coping messages.

redFlags: Temperature 38 °C or more under 3 months (NICE NG143)
Bilious vomiting, blood in stool or a distended abdomen
Poor feeding, faltering weight, floppiness or drowsiness
High-pitched or weak cry, bulging fontanelle
Groin or scrotal swelling; hair tourniquet
psychosocial: Parental exhaustion and sense of failure
ice: Concern: a missed illness and her own coping

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Noah has colic. I’ve examined him fully and he’s a healthy, thriving baby.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Colic means long bouts of crying in a well baby. We don’t fully know why it happens, but it isn’t harmful, it isn’t anything you’ve done, and it usually settles by three to four months.”

management.reflectIce: “You were terrified something serious was wrong. I’ve checked him from head to toe, and he’s well. Now I want to make sure you’re okay too.”
management.psychosocial: Validate her exhaustion; ask about mood and anxiety; explicit permission to put him down safely.
sharedPlan: Reassurance and soothing strategies; no routine drops or formula changes
ICON information; never-shake and walk-away advice
Health visitor visit; review of parental mood (NICE CG192)
safetyNet: Temperature 38 °C or more, poor feeding, green vomit, blood in nappy, floppiness or change in cry: urgent review or 111
Feeling unable to cope or low mood: contact the practice or health visitor the same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The diagnosis is easy; the marks are in how safely you reach it and how well you look after the parent. Candidates fail by skipping the examination, by medicalising crying, and by never asking about the mother.

items.why: Colic is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection, hernia, torsion and hair tourniquet must be ruled out.
items.fix: Examine fully undressed and plot the weight.

items.fail: Prescribing drops, reflux medicine or a new formula.
items.why: Evidence is limited, and crying alone is not an indication for acid suppression (NICE NG1).
items.fix: Reassure and give soothing strategies; consider allergy only with other features (NICE CG116).

items.why: Crying is a recognised trigger for abusive head trauma.
items.fix: Give the ICON message, including permission to walk away safely.

items.why: Her exhaustion and anxiety are the hidden agenda, and postnatal mood matters (NICE CG192).
items.fix: Ask how she is, screen mood and anxiety, and arrange support.

items.why: Early reassurance sounds dismissive and may be wrong.
items.fix: Examine first, then reassure with the findings.

items.why: A febrile baby under 3 months needs same-day assessment (NICE NG143).
items.fix: Name the red flags and the 38 °C threshold, and book review.
